---

### 🎯 Practical Learning Objectives

- **Draw** simple random, stratified and systematic samples.
- **Observe** sampling variability and the standard error.
- **Demonstrate** how a biased sampling method distorts an estimate.

---

## 1. The Population

We treat the 4,257 simulated retail sales as the **population**, so we know the true mean and can see how well each sampling method estimates it.

```{r load}
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
pop <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "retail_sales_ng.csv"))
true_mean <- mean(pop$Sales_Amount)
c(N = nrow(pop), true_mean = true_mean)
```

---

## 2. Three Sampling Methods

```{r methods}
set.seed(42)
srs   <- slice_sample(pop, n = 200)                                   # simple random
strat <- pop |> group_by(Region) |> slice_sample(n = 40) |> ungroup() # stratified: 40 per region
k     <- floor(nrow(pop) / 200)
sys   <- pop[seq(sample(k, 1), nrow(pop), by = k), ]                  # systematic: every k-th row

tibble(method = c("Simple random", "Stratified", "Systematic"),
       n = c(nrow(srs), nrow(strat), nrow(sys)),
       estimate = c(mean(srs$Sales_Amount), mean(strat$Sales_Amount), mean(sys$Sales_Amount)),
       error = estimate - true_mean)
```

Stratified sampling gives equal numbers from each region, so unless regions have the same size it needs **weights** to estimate the population mean. Here the regions differ in size, so the unweighted stratified mean is not an unbiased estimate of the population mean.

## 3. Sampling Variability and the Standard Error

One sample gives one estimate. Repeating the sampling shows how much estimates vary.

```{r se}
set.seed(42)
means <- replicate(1000, mean(slice_sample(pop, n = 200)$Sales_Amount))
c(mean_of_means = mean(means), empirical_SE = sd(means),
  theory_SE = sd(pop$Sales_Amount) / sqrt(200))

ggplot(tibble(means), aes(means)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Sampling distribution of the mean (n = 200)", x = "Sample mean", y = "Count")
```

The distribution is centred on the true mean (red line) and its spread is the **standard error**, $SE = \sigma / \sqrt{n}$. (The simulation samples without replacement from a finite population, so it is slightly smaller than the formula.)

## 4. Sampling Bias

```{r bias}
biased <- pop |> arrange(desc(Sales_Amount)) |> slice_head(n = 200)    # only the biggest sales are "surveyed"
c(true_mean = true_mean, biased_mean = mean(biased$Sales_Amount))
```

## 5. Summary and Reflection

- Random sampling gives estimates centred on the truth; the spread shrinks with $\sqrt{n}$.
- Stratified sampling guarantees representation but needs weights.
- Bias cannot be removed by a bigger sample.

> 🧠 **Reflection:** Name two sources of bias in a survey of student opinions carried out only in the university library on a Monday morning.
